newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan rescuers seek children trapped by quake.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan rescuers seek children trapped by quake.

text.p: Using their bare hands to heave aside rubble, rescuers in eastern Venezuela on Thursday searched for dozens of children trapped in classrooms ruined by a powerful quake that killed at least 59 people.
"The total number of deaths confirmed now is 59, with 322 injured," Sucre State Governor Ramon Martinez told reporters.
Schools and office buildings were razed by the tremor -- measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale -- crushing the children as they took end-of-term exams. Authorities said the death toll could rise.
Victims ranged from infants to the elderly. Another 500 families were left homeless by the South American nation's worst earthquake for three decades.
President Rafael Caldera announced three days of national mourning. He was due to inspect the rescue operation.
More than 20 hours after the first tremor, survivors were being pulled from rubble.

The small agricultural town Cariaco about 295 miles (470 km) east of Caracas, took the brunt. Scores of homes and buildings were flattened, including two schools, killing at least 41, mostly children.
One resident recounted pulling a young girl from the wreckage of a house. "She was talking to me as we walked and, all of a sudden, I turned around and she was dead," he said.
Dozens of distraught family members milled in the street facing the Raimundo Martinez Centeno high school, staring blankly as rescue workers picked through the ruins.
Textbooks and broken desks lay scattered. Several limbs could be seen in the bloodied rubble.

For many of the pupils, Thursday was to be their last day before the summer break. "Some of them were taking end of term exams," said arts teacher Tomas Pantoja as he tried to rescue a student with crippling leg and arm wounds.
Thanks to a sore throat, Oscar Rodriguez, 15, survived, telling a Reuters correspondent, "I wasn't going to go because I was ill but a teacher convinced me."
Tears in his eyes, Rodriquez said, "When I was arriving the building started to move as if it was on a wave and the whole thing crashed down."
Survivors said eight of the school's 12 classrooms were in use at the time of the quake, and four caved in. "The building collapsed as if it had been hit by a bomb," Pantoja said.
In the historic state capital Cumana, 40 miles (60 km) west, rescue efforts concentrated on a six-story office building that fell like a pack of cards.
Martinez said at least 11 bodies were pulled from the ruins and another 30 rescued alive.
"We don't know how many people are still in there but we know there are a lot because the quake hit during office hours," Jose Azocar, Cumana's fire chief, told reporters.

Firemen and medics swarmed over the rubble, removing debris and trying to keep contact with those buried. Cranes and trucks stood by to remove the rubble. Stray scraps of office stationery fluttered around the site.
Around dawn on Thursday a group clustered near one of the holes opened in the wreckage burst into cheers and applause. Shortly afterwards a woman was carried away on a stretcher.
One group of survivors, trapped in the basement, kept in contact with the outside world by cellular telephones, Martinez said.
Up to 70 people were thought to have been in the building at the time of the quake.
Hospitals were overwhelmed by the flood of injured.

"Most of those hurt were children and have lost their legs and arms after they were taken from the ruins and then given very rudimentary surgery," said Ramon Ward, director of Cariaco's 30-bed Diego Carbonel hospital which has treated hundreds of patients since Wednesday afternoon.
Witnesses said the agricultural town of 13,000 was destroyed: streets riven by huge cracks and the traditional mud-walled houses flattened.
Urban Development Minister Julio Marti said very early estimates put the cost of infrastructural damage at $8 million.
The quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck about 3:25 p.m. EDT (1925 GMT) Wednesday.
The FUNVISIS seismological institute said the first quake measured 6.9 on the open-ended Richter scale.
The epicentre was about 30 miles (49 km) off Venezuela's northeastern Caribbean coast and there were at least 15 aftershocks, the last in the early hours Thursday.
State-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela said production and export continued to flow smoothly. Venezuela is the largest exporter of crude oil to the United States.

Founded in 1521, Cumana is the oldest inhabited city in South America. However, most of its colonial architecture was destroyed in a massive earthquake in 1766. Wednesday's earthquake was the second major tremor to strike the city of 250,000 people this century, the last in 1929.
The 1967 quake, the last to cause serious damage in Venezuela, killed 215 in the capital and surrounding area, FUNVISIS officials said.
